column4: The section’s source dictionary notes the sun-name الإلاهة because people worshiped it; 41:37 directly forbids سجود to sun and moon and directs سجود to their Creator, sharpening إياك نعبد.

The source dictionary’s sun-name الإلاهة is tied to worship; the Hudhud reports people سجود للشمس من دون الله and says this held them from السبيل, joining the image’s sun cult to Fatiha’s path and guidance.
In Abraham’s test of celestial lights, the star sets (أفل), and he says لا أحب الآفلين; a visible light’s disappearance defeats treating it as Lord.
Abraham watches the moon set, then says لئن لم يهدني ربي لأكونن من القوم الضالين; this passage itself gathers Rab, guidance, and the lost people named in the section’s Fatiha reading.
Abraham calls the rising sun “greater,” but when it sets (أفلت) he disavows the objects they associate with God; the same test now uses the sun.

After the sun sets, Abraham turns his face to the One who created the heavens and earth (فطر السماوات والأرض); this gives the section’s worship distinction its creator, rather than a heavenly light, as its object.
The cave passage stages the sun shifting away at rising and setting (تزاور … تقرضهم), then says من يهد الله فهو المهتد; it joins the image’s moving sunlight to its guidance theme.

In Abraham’s argument about lordship, the challenge فأت بها من المغرب turns the sun’s rising from the east into evidence against the ruler who disputes God; the luminary’s course belongs to the Creator.

Following 27:24’s sun worship, the Hudhud asks them to سجود to Allah, who brings forth the hidden in the heavens and earth; the neighbour completes the contrast by naming the rightful recipient of prostration.
The verse explicitly lists الشمس والقمر among those who prostrate to Allah; it reverses the human act of prostrating to the sun in the section.
The section develops the rising crescent and lunar stations; 2:189 calls the الأهلة time markers (مواقيت) for people and pilgrimage, making the crescent a calendar sign.
This verse names the sun’s radiance, the moon’s light, and its stations (منازل) for counting years and حساب; it directly supplies the timekeeping purpose behind the section’s lunar-mansion image.
The verse says the moon was measured in stations (منازل) until it returns like an old date stalk; this gives the crescent and the section’s named lunar mansion a visible phase cycle.
Dhul-Qarnayn reaches the setting place of the sun (مغرب الشمس); the scene gives a second concrete horizon image for the section’s daylight span from sunrise to sunset.
Dhul-Qarnayn reaches the rising place of the sun (مطلع الشمس), pairing with 18:86 and the section’s sunrise-to-sunset definition of yawm.

The source’s q-w-m dictionary image says the noon sun stands overhead while the shadow nearly disappears; 25:45 instead describes shadow extended and the sun as its دليل, giving the changing shadow that makes the noon image perceptible.
The next verse says God draws the shadow back gradually (قبضناه … قبضا يسيرا); after 25:45’s sun-as-guide, it completes the shadow’s motion around the section’s near-shadowless noon.
The source’s q-w-m gloss pictures noon with almost no shadow to right or left; 16:48 depicts shadows inclining on both sides (عن اليمين والشمائل), a specific contrast within the day’s movement.
The verse says created shadows prostrate to God at morning and evening (ظلالهم بالغدو والآصال); against human prostration to the sun, even the image’s changing shade is placed in submission to God.

The section’s q-w-m dictionary includes ميزان النهار standing in balance; 55:7 places the balance (الميزان) alongside the raised sky, giving a Qur’anic counterpart while using balance in its own cosmic measure sense.
الشمس والقمر بحسبان gives the sun and moon an ordered calculation; it complements the section’s measured day and lunar stations.
The verse says the sun runs to its appointed course (لمستقر لها); the visible sun in the section’s day-long sky is itself moving within a measured limit.
The verse says the sun cannot overtake the moon and each moves in an orbit; it gives the two lights distinct bounds rather than divine independence.
This verse joins dawn splitting, night as rest, and sun and moon by calculation (حسبانا); it makes the section’s day and luminaries part of an ordered time system.

After describing creation of heaven and earth and night covering day, the verse says sun, moon, and stars are subjected to God’s command; their celestial motion is created service, not a reason to worship them.
The verse says God raised the heavens and subjected sun and moon, each running to a stated term; it directly places the section’s lights under the Creator’s rule.
The verse says sun and moon are subjected in their continuous courses and night and day are subjected too; it joins the section’s two celestial lights to its full daily cycle.
Night, day, sun, moon, and stars are all subjected by God’s command; this repeats the section’s sky scene while identifying the lights as governed signs.
The verse names night, day, sun, and moon and says each swims in an orbit (فلك); it supplies the moving celestial order behind the image of a sky turning through the day.
Asked who created the heavens and earth and subjected sun and moon, the people answer Allah; the passage makes the worshiped luminary answer to its Creator.
The verse describes night entering day and day entering night, then sun and moon running to a term; it expands the image from noon to the alternating cycle that contains it.
Night and day enter one another while sun and moon run to a stated term; the verse presents the section’s celestial lights as bounded parts of God’s order.
God wraps night over day and day over night and subjects sun and moon to a term; this gives the section’s turning sky its explicit cycle and limit.
The verse makes night and day two signs, the day visible for seeking provision, and their sequence a means to count years and calculation; it concretizes the section’s yawm as measurable daylight.
The verse pairs creation of the heavens and earth with the succession of night and day (اختلاف الليل والنهار); it presents the section’s turning sky as a sign for reflection.
The succession of night and day and what God created in the heavens and earth are signs; this directly links the image’s daily sky cycle to its encompassing celestial sphere.
This verse places constellations in the sky together with a lamp and a shining moon; it concretely fills the section’s dictionary image of the sky as a sphere and what it contains.
The verse calls the moon a light and the sun a lamp (نورًا … سراجًا); it gives the image’s two visible lights distinct created roles.
The verse calls the sun a blazing lamp (سراجا وهاجا), a direct image of the daylight sun that the section distinguishes from God.
The oath by the sun and its brightness (الشمس وضحاها) directly stages the daylight light at the center of this image.
The next oath names the moon when it follows the sun (والقمر إذا تلاها); it places the section’s sun and moon in one observed sky sequence.
The next oath names day when it displays the sun (والنهار إذا جلاها); it states the day-and-sun relation that the section develops through sunrise, noon, and sunset.
The following oath names night when it covers the sun (والليل إذا يغشاها), completing the day-to-night arc around the section’s daylight image.
The section’s dictionary gloss defines the sky as what is above and shelters; 21:32 calls the sky a protected ceiling (سقفا محفوظا), a close Qur’anic image of that covering.
The verse describes seven heavens layered above (سماوات طباقا); it concretizes the section’s named sky as an encompassing upper sphere.
Prayer begins at the sun’s decline (لدلوك الشمس) and continues to night, with dawn named separately; this marks the daily course around the section’s noon sun.
The verse names praise to God at evening and when people enter noon (حين تظهرون); it makes noon, where the section’s sun stands overhead, a time of worship directed to God.
On the Day of Resurrection the moon is darkened (خسف القمر); this is a stated boundary to the ordinary lunar light and stations in the image, and 75:9 joins the sun and moon.
The next verse says the sun and moon are joined (جمع الشمس والقمر) at Resurrection, reversing the distinct courses and stations of the image’s two lights.
At the cosmic end, the sun is rolled up (الشمس كورت); this reverses the ordinary daylight course that the section follows from rising to setting.
The next verse says the stars grow dim or fall away (النجوم انكدرت); it extends the same end-time reversal to the celestial contents surrounding the section’s sun and moon.
The sky splits open (السماء انفطرت) at the Day of Judgment, reversing the section’s dictionary image of an overhead sheltering sky.
The next verse says the stars scatter (الكواكب انتثرت), extending the sky’s opening to the luminaries contained in the section’s celestial sphere.
Immediately before the star test, God shows Abraham the kingdom of the heavens and earth (ملكوت السماوات والأرض); this supplies the celestial setting for 6:76 and locates it within God’s display.
The verse just before the sun-worship report says a woman rules the people (امرأة تملكهم); it adds the specific political setting that the section notes for 27:24.
After the Hudhud’s report and call to prostrate to Allah, this verse says Allah alone is God and Lord of the great throne; it completes the report’s contrast between the sun and its Lord.

After the shadow passage, the verse pairs night as a covering with day as renewed activity (الليل لباسا … النهار نشورا); it carries the sun-and-shadow sequence into the other half of the section’s day cycle.
After 16:48’s moving shadows prostrate to God, this verse says all creatures in heaven and earth and the angels prostrate to Him; it widens the same submission scene beyond shadows.
The verse after the balance is set warns not to transgress it (ألا تطغوا في الميزان); it shows the Quranic measure’s moral use, distinct from the source dictionary’s balanced-noon image.
The next verse commands just weight and not diminishing the balance (وأقيموا الوزن بالقسط); it completes the passage’s move from the section’s day-balance dictionary image to measured justice.
The section’s dictionary gloss treats the sky as what stands above and shelters; 40:64 calls it a structure (السماء بناء) above the settled earth, another concrete overhead image.
The source dictionary describes the sky as what is above and shelters; 2:22 calls it a structure (السماء بناء) over the earth in its account of provision and creation.
The verse says God built seven strong heavens above people (فوقكم سبعا شدادا); this gives the section’s covering sky a layered, built form.
The command to glorify God before sunrise and before sunset (قبل طلوع الشمس وقبل غروبها) places worship at the two boundaries of the section’s sun-defined day.
The verse tells the Prophet to glorify God before sunrise and before sunset; it places worship of God at the same solar boundaries used to define the section’s daylight.
The following verse continues glorification through the night and after prostration; it completes the solar-boundary worship in 50:39 with the night side of the cycle.
The verse places prayer at the day’s two ends and near parts of the night; it maps worship onto the daylight interval whose middle the section identifies with noon.
The verse makes night and day succeed one another (خلفة) for remembrance or gratitude; it names the recurring cycle that surrounds the section’s noon and daylight.
The verse says النجم and trees prostrate; النجم can mean a star or a low-growing plant, so the celestial reading is uncertain, but it would reverse treating a heavenly light as an object of worship.
